analysis.one_liner: Repeals OSHA's power to inspect workplaces, issue citations, and fine employers who violate safety rules.
analysis.headline: A bill to strip OSHA of its inspection, citation, and penalty powers drew 20 Republican cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the sections of the Occupational Safety and Health Act that let OSHA inspect workplaces, issue citations, and impose civil and criminal penalties on employers who break safety rules. It would have replaced that enforcement system with voluntary tools: a small-business consulting program, awards for companies with good safety records, and a requirement that every new safety rule pass a cost-benefit test. It also would have declared that employer-run safety committees do not count as "labor organizations" under federal labor law.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially in hazardous industries, would gain the most: no more OSHA inspections, citations, or fines, and a higher cost-benefit bar before any new safety standard could take effect. Small businesses would also gain a guaranteed consulting and training program funded by at least one-fourth of OSHA's budget. Companies with strong safety records could win a government award they may use in advertising.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the OSH Act covering inspections, investigations, recordkeeping, citations, enforcement procedures, judicial review, and civil and criminal penalties, leaving workplace safety standards without any mandatory enforcement mechanism.

Raises the bar for new standards: the Labor Secretary would have to find each rule addresses a significant risk, is feasible, has a reasonable relationship between costs and benefits, and is the most cost-effective way to protect workers while minimizing job losses in the affected industry.

Declares that employee safety and health committees are not 'labor organizations' under the National Labor Relations Act, allowing employers to set up workplace safety committees without them becoming union bargaining units.

Requires that at least one-fourth of OSHA's annual appropriation be spent on technical assistance and consultative services targeted at small employers and the most hazardous industries, and creates a government award for companies with outstanding safety programs that they may publicize in advertising.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear the cost: with inspections, citations, penalties, and judicial review repealed, OSHA standards could no longer be enforced against employers who ignore them, so compliance would depend entirely on voluntary cooperation. Workers would also lose the protection that keeps employer-run safety committees from functioning as company-controlled substitutes for unions.

drawbacks.text: By repealing the provisions for inspections, citations, enforcement, and penalties, the bill leaves OSHA standards with no mechanism to compel compliance; an employer could ignore a safety rule with no legal consequence.

The new cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness findings required for every standard could slow or block new workplace protections, particularly rules whose benefits to workers' health are real but hard to quantify in dollars.

Declaring employer safety committees exempt from the National Labor Relations Act would let companies run management-dominated committees without union involvement, removing a safeguard against committees that exist to keep unions out rather than to protect workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's assistance program, consulting services, and safety awards have genuine value, and prioritizing hazards by the number of workers exposed is sensible. But those tools are all voluntary. The bill's main effect is to remove the only compulsory tools OSHA had — inspections, citations, and fines — so its benefit to employers comes chiefly from no longer being made to comply, while the risk of noncompliance shifts entirely onto the workers the standards are supposed to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House committee that handles labor law, then to a subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing or vote until the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joel Hefley introduced the bill on January 26, 1995, with 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities.
On February 10, 1995, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where no further action was taken.
Hefley gave introductory remarks again on July 9, 1996, roughly a year and a half after introduction, but the bill never advanced to a markup or floor vote.
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers came out ahead: OSHA kept its inspection, citation, and penalty powers, so safety standards remained legally enforceable. Employers did not get the relief from inspections and fines the bill would have provided.

for.name: Rep. Joel Hefley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor twice, in January 1995 and again in July 1996, trying to move it.

for.name: 20 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 20 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee on February 10, 1995, and never took it up for a markup or vote; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed 1995 efforts to weaken or repeal OSHA's inspection and penalty authority, arguing enforcement is what keeps safety standards meaningful.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; since it never reached a vote, there is no roll call to show how the chambers would have split.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking)
industries.note: The bill repeals OSHA's inspection, citation, enforcement, and penalty provisions, so employers in the most dangerous lines of work would no longer face fines or mandatory inspections for unsafe conditions. Their gain comes directly out of workers' protection.

The bill declares employer safety committees are not 'labor organizations' under the NLRA, weakening a union safeguard against company-run committees and making it easier for employers to deal with workers outside collective bargaining.

Small employers would get a guaranteed consulting and training program funded by at least a quarter of OSHA's budget, plus relief from citations and penalties. Some of this genuinely helps them make their workplaces safer voluntarily.
The bill authorizes OSHA to deliver assistance directly or by grant or contract, opening a funded channel for consulting services to small and hazardous-workplace employers.
